# Summary

We compare a dummy classifier, a decision tree, logistic regression, and a support vector classifier on a seven-class weight-status prediction task. The models use demographic, family history, and lifestyle variables from the UCI Obesity Levels dataset, with height and weight excluded. About 77% of the published records are synthetic, which limits what performance on this dataset can tell us about performance on independently collected survey data.

# Introduction

Researchers have compared machine learning models for classifying weight status from survey data, including models that use both eating habits and physical measurements ([Kaur et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12020-022-03215-4) and [Solomon et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.3390/diagnostics13152610)). For this dataset, the authors calculated body mass index (BMI) from height and weight and used it to assign the weight-status labels ([Mendoza Palechor & de la Hoz Manotas, 2019](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dib.2019.104344)). Excluding those measurements and any features derived from them lets us test how much predictive information comes from the remaining survey responses.

Our research question is: **How well can demographic, family history, and lifestyle features predict the seven weight-status categories when height and weight are excluded, and which of the four classifiers performs best?** Comparing the classifiers against a dummy baseline shows whether using these survey responses improves predictions over a simple benchmark.

We use the [UCI Obesity Levels dataset (2019)](https://doi.org/10.24432/C5H31Z), which contains 2,111 records based on an online survey conducted in Mexico, Peru, and Colombia. Each row describes one individual or is a synthetic record generated from the survey data. The candidate predictors include age, gender, family history of overweight, eating habits, physical activity, and other behaviours such as usual transportation. The response is the recorded weight-status category: insufficient weight, normal weight, overweight level I or II, or obesity type I, II, or III.
